(Australia) I 25f grew up in an ubuse/neglect situation. I didn't honestly know that dental care was even a real thing until my late teens. My parents nor siblings didn't do it, siblings and myself were never taught. By the time I started the damage was already done and getting worse.

What are my options going forward? Can anyone explain the process of going to a dentist? Do you tell them what you want to do before the appointment? Do they have set prices? Im in a tough spot financially so I'm scared of getting a higher than anticipated bill. I'm confused by the whole process. I've only been to a dentist once as an adult when I had sepsis from an infected wisdom tooth thus don't really remember the experience. Please help. Any advice is welcome.

Patient information: Age 25, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
I agree with some of the advice that others have given already! 

Just want to add that it's extremely common for people to be nervous about going to the dentist, especially if you haven't been often. Dentists know this, and should be supportive throughout. You can let them know that you are nervous or that you haven't seen a dentist recently. 

You should be able to phone local dentists and discuss with reception what the pricing is for a regular check up. At your first appointment they can explain what other treatments they recommend and how much they cost. 

Its hard to find free dental care in Aus, but clinics will have different prices, and they can give you that information before your appointment. 

I think it's great that you want to see a dentist and have your teeth looked at. Good luck OP!


Edit: This website has info about public dental services if you are based in NSW:

https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/oralhealth/Pages/info-patients.aspx#appointments

21M | 170cm | 67kg | Non-smoker | Alcohol once a month or less | GERD, anxiety |

Hey! For 2-3 years now i have had a very low pulse imo. In the beginnig of this i didnt eat much and i went from 86kg down to 55kg, because of health anxiety. Im much better now. Im not super athletic at all, i only go for 1-2 walks a day for 1 hour +. I dont work atm and im usually at home. Last BP was 130/66. I had 2 ECGs in july, they were good. 

So, i can have a full blown panick attack and my pulse will still be like 46-60 and i breathe very slow, feels like i cant "normally" breathe faster. My pulse increases when i stand and when i walk etc and ive had like 166 when walking up a hill, i never get tired, and i walk fast. 

Peak Flow Meter is 500-600 and my Spo2 is always 97-99%. The problem is that it just feels so weak and slow when im wide awake and have panick attacks, shouldnt it go up when im like that, and hyperventilate? Im the complete opposite. My doc told me its alright, i have been there several times, and my heart and lungs sounds fine. She told me that i had no need to go to a cardiologist unless i started passing out occasionally etc. 

Why is it like this? Am i just in better shape then i think? The anxiety one is just weird for me. I have GERD and alot of muscle tension throughout my body. Im usually not dizzy when i have low pulse, i feel alright, just scared and anxious about it. Been hard to breathe these 3 years but always normal Spo2. 

Dont know what more info could be relevant.

Patient information: Age 21, Gender: M
provided_physician_response:
Young, relatively healthy people commonly have low resting heart rates. Your heart is just more "efficient" when it's younger and not abused from decades of high blood pressure. So I wouldn't continue worrying about your heart right now. 

I do encourage you to focus that anxiety, though. Panic attacks suck and I wish you all the best.

D-dimer is a byproduct of clot formation, so anytime a clot forms some d-dimer will form as well. The bigger the clot the more the d-dimer. Naturally the body is constantly forming clots from microtrauma to blood vessels due to normal wear and tear. But also after getting an injury, like blood drawn for lab work. Ultimately that means that you will always have some d-dimer amount in your blood. Which is what makes it a horrible test in most applications, very sensitive to almost anything and very not specific to almost anything.

Troponin is a protein that is part of muscle, in your case they were looking for cardiac troponin (from the heart). It is only supposed to be in the heart muscle cells. If any of it is in the blood that means there was heart muscle breakdown and the troponin "leaked" into the blood from within the muscle cells of the heart. The more heart muscle damage, the higher the troponin level. So ideally you should have none in your blood.

This is an oversimplification but the gist of it.

45F, white, 125 pounds. I see warnings that you can not get an SGB if you have a cold, flu, fever, or active infection. Why is this? I have a block scheduled for Monday and have a bit of a cold. No fever, just a bit stuffy etc. what would happen if I still got the block?

Patient information: Age 45, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
So the other user was saying to call your anesthesia provider because SGB are often done by an anesthesiologist who is interventional pain management trained.

As for your question: having an infection can theoretically lead to spread when the needle passes through tissue that may be involved with the infection.

As an example, if a woman wants an epidural for labor, an infection or even cancer over the lower back is considered unsafe for an epidural. Again, if a needle passes through the affected tissues, you can theoretically get spread.

As such, a cold is generally short-lived and it is reasonable to wait the short time to get over the illness and then do the block. Vs. risking possible spread. 

Hope that helps.

Getting to the solution is a high priority in my life as its debilitating, and I'm getting stressed out its taken so long to get a simple interpretation of the results.

Here are the results. Can anyone here give me any insight?

Also, any thoughts on how to deal with a Dr who's ghosted?

After 12 hour water and food deprivation:

Urine Osmolality - 438

Blood Osmolality - 291

Sodium, random urine - 35

Glucose - 100

BUN - 13

Creatinine - 1.06

Sodium - 141

Potassium - 4.5

Chloride - 100

CO2 - 23

Calcium - 9.7

eGFR - 89

Patient information: Age 44, Gender: M
provided_physician_response:
It's been a long time since I tested for DI, but I believe your testing may be incomplete.  After the fluid restriction, you didn't meet the urine osmolality (>700) that would have definitively meant Primary Polydipsia.  

You would probably need a hypertonic saline infusion until you reach one of two end points, sodium > 145 or urine osmolality > 700.  If the urine osmolality criteria is the end point you reach then you would have Primary Polydipsia.  If the sodium criteria is what you reach, you'd need a desmopressin stimulation test, and based on that result you could determine which type, if any, diabetes insipidus you may have.  That test could also show that you have Primary Polydipsia if there was minimal response to the desmopressin.

I am 45/F/5'3/180ish. I have been deaf since birth, progressively. Taking Prozac 20mg, Wellbutrin 150mg, Propranolol prn. In 2013 (age 35) I got a cochlear implant in my right ear. All was going well until I started having facial twitching when wearing the device and shocks inside my head. After some back and forth with my clinic I decided to just stop using it and move on. 

Since then I've had the following symptoms slowly grow worse or become more consistent. I've been diagnosed with depression, anxiety, slightly enlarged left thyroid, generalized fatigue/hypersomnia. I saw an ENT in Nov 2021 who felt a lump on the right side of my neck and had a CT done. My complaints and reason for seeing the ENT included headaches, neck pain, very visible asymmetrical swelling on my right neck/jawline, mild swallowing difficulties/chronic cough (I've had a cough since 2019). These were the findings:

2021 FINDINGS: No definite CT evidence of a discrete mass within the right parotid gland. No definite evidence of disproportionate enhancement, radiopaque calculi or ductal dilatation to the parotid gland on the right. Submandibular glands, muscles of mastication, tongue, floor of mouth, pharynx, larynx appear unremarkable. No definite enlarged lymph nodes within the neck. Few phleboliths noted within the palatine tonsils. Asymmetry in the size of the thyroid glands with the right appearing larger than the left. No definite CT evidence of a discrete nodule within the thyroid. Streak artifact coursing through the thyroid from the patient shoulders. Nasal septum deviated to the right with a prominent spur abutting the inferior turbinate. Paranasal sinuses appear unopacified. Partial mastoidectomy changes noted on the right with a metallic device extending into the middle ear cavity incompletely seen on this study. Partial opacification of the remaining inferior mastoid air cells. Prominent degenerative changes within the cervical spine most pronounced at C5-C6 and C6-C7. Mild to moderate neural foramina narrowing on the right  at C5-C6.

IMPRESSION:
1. No definite CT evidence of a discrete mass within the parotid gland.
2. Mild nonspecific enlargement of the thyroid on the right relative to the left.
3. Partial mastoidectomy changes noted on the right with a metallic device extending into the middle ear cavity.

_____________
My ENT wrote "no discreet mass was noted. I think it was fullness of the SCM in that area you are feeling. Have a nice day!" The doctor then rejected my request for a follow up appointment. I didn't feel a lump, she did! I went in for neck pain and headaches and she found the lump. 

I wrote down everything I've complained about in the last five years and finally made the connection this was all probably due to cochlear implant failure/migration. I don't see the doctor frequently (why bother?) but when I do they give me more antidepressants. I had bad anxiety for awhile in 2020, but have no emotional or cognitive complaints. 

After a month and 11 follow up calls I finally got an appointment to begin the removal process at Mayo Clinic, where it was implanted. I am also having a sleep study done in November. I had a home one done and have mild apnea (6 incidents per hour) that shouldn't be making me fatigued/hypersomniac. 

I need someone to review the big picture and let me know if I sound crazy. I want to know if all of this will go away with the explanation or if I'm doomed to have a fat right jawline and neck for the rest of my life. I also want to know how mad I should be at my doctors. Thanks!

Patient information: Age 45, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
Nothing you are experiencing is due to the cochlear implant, and it doesn't really sound like it failed. It isn't uncommon to have some stimulation of the facial nerve with the device. An audiologist fixes that by changing the electrode stimulations such that it doesn't do that. If there are zaps or other concerning things, an audiologist can interrogate it to determine what is going on. You may be perceiving facial stimulation as zaps. Either way, this wouldn't have anything to do with what you are experiencing in the neck. 

I don't know what's going on in the neck, the CT was unremarkable and your physician didn't seem to find anything that was concerning. Without an examination can't say much more.

29M 5'8" 165lbs. Don't smoke, drink or do drugs.

On 10/14 I had 3 wisdom teeth removed. My top 2 wisdom teeth had been emerged for years, my bottom left tooth was impacted and had began an infection 1 week prior, and I di not have a lower right wisdom tooth.
All 3 were extracted on 10/14. I've been healing well and careful with what I eat, only eating more solid foods in the last 2-3 days.

When my infection started I was prescribed amoxicillin 500mg 4x/day. I did that until my surgery, after which I was prescribed penicillin 500mg 4x/day. I had taken the penicillin up until 2 days ago, when I stopped (so 4-5 days after surgery). I don't like the harmful, sometimes permanent effects that destroying your gut microbiome can have and I want to mitigate that as much as possible.

I started getting paranoid about getting an infection in the lower left again and I took a penicillin, thinking I'd run it for another 2-3 days. But then I thought, what if I broke a pill and placed it gently directly on the socket that I'm worried about.

Would this be effective at treating it locally and mitigating the systemic effects of the antibiotics? As I said, I have both amoxicillin and penicillin, if one is somehow better than the other.

To be clear, I am asking about the efficacy of my proposal. I'm not interested in hearing about how some of you might think that the gut microbiome is a non-factor.

PS: Is there a better of the 2, between amoxicillin and penicillin to use for my situation? Be it orally or my proposed topical solution?

Patient information: Age 29, Gender: M
provided_physician_response:
Topical would not be effective. It is very important to complete the entire antibiotic regimen as prescribed to prevent antibiotic resistance and ensure the infection gets treated completely. 

Your concerns about your gut microbiome are not unfounded and antibiotics can cause diarrheal illness. There is [data](https://www.singlecare.com/blog/taking-probiotics-with-antibiotics/) to support using a probiotic during your antibiotic course to prevent diarrheal illness while taking the antibiotic. This would be a better approach to treating your infection with proper antibiotic use and limiting your risk.

The new spot in your chest (the hilar node) may or may not be significant. There are other things that can cause a node to light up on PET scan. The presence of calcifications in a node is usually an indication of benign causes, rather than malignant causes of hypermetabolic activity. Patient information: Age 62, Gender: M
provided_physician_response:
There is a degree of cardiac remodelling that can take place after a heart attack (which you might regard as "healing") but many of the interventions post-MI are more about secondary prevention; that is, preventing another heart attack.

The heart muscle will never be 100% again, but you can still live a normal, healthy life after a heart attack and having had one does not always mean you will end up with heart failure. Preventing further episodes is the big thing, as subsequent heart attacks will increase risk of long-term complications exponentially.

provided_physician_response:
How long do you have left until you return home? 

In areas with low risk it is fine to just have the emergency treatment and take it when you start feeling symptoms. In high-risk areas it would be better to take the prophylactic dose. Personally I'd probably gravitate to not stretching them out and risk having neither are working prophylactic dose nor a working emergency dose. Then there's also a consideration that in more urban areas area, you might be able to receive proper treatment in the hospital if you get infected. In countries where malaria is common, the doctors are usually also experienced with treatment. Obviously it depends on where exactly you are, and if you're in a very rural area, you might be out of luck.

If you can use your tablets to keep up the proper prophylactic dose until 1 1/2 weeks before returning, that might be a good option, because as far as I know the incubation period for malaria usually is around two weeks, so if you return and start feeling sick, you can get proper treatment at home. 

If you are staying for a longer time, I would really recommend trying to find medication on location to replace what you gave away. Otherwise keeping the emergency dose is probably not a bad idea. There's always concerns about fake meds unfortunately, but in areas where Malaria is common, you should be possible to get the meds at a pharmacy.

You seem to be doing well with the whole preventative measures like mosquito netting, behavioural choices etc., so keep that up. Not getting stung/bitten is the best protection, and if you have spent some time down there, you probably have minimising exposure down well.

I might not be on top of my malaria game, so if someone else could chime in, that be great. Take care!

Hi all!

My wife (34F) suffers from chronic pain and has many of the symptoms of migraine or cluster headache: mainly on one side, face pain around the sinuses and jaw, photophobia, pain at the base of the neck.

She also has other long standing pain issues in her shoulder, shoulder blade, and down to her mid back on the same side. 

Not looking for a diagnosis but I can't seem to understand how almost all of her ailments are so much better on 50mg sumatriptan (prescribed by doctor). 

The headache and face pain makes sense, as does the photophobia , but the sumatriptan also seems to help with neck, shoulder and general upper back pain. Her overall mood seems better (no doubt because she's in less pain). It's almost a miracle - on days with no sumatriptan she's bed-bound, but on days where she takes it, she can almost live a life again. 

Could her shoulder, neck and upper/mid back pain be related to migraine/cluster headaches? So by helping with the origin of the pain, the sumatriptan helps with other areas? 

Also, am I correct in understanding that sumatriptan specifically works on migraine/cluster headaches and nothing else? 

Thanks, trying to make sense of why this works while also struggling to get GP appointments that aren't weeks away.

Patient information: Age 34, Gender: F
provided_physician_response: She should ask about a CGRP antagonist like Emgality if she's needing to use sumatriptan this frequently. Many get migraines from cranial nerve dysfunction, most notably the trigeminal nerve which can cause all sorts of funky, very painful sensations to occur. Triptans do work well for migraines and act at the level of the blood vessels in the brain stop them from spasming. Newer drugs like CGRP antagonists actually help to calm the nerves that are inflamed. She might benefit from this if she is having so many extra cranial nerve issues as well. Some with migraines get more widespread symptoms, which can even affect the GI tract. If triptans work this well for her functionality, it's time to find something preventative, not just abortive meaning chasing symptoms instead of preventing them.

On my bottle of children's advil (100 mg/5 ml) it says the dosing for 4-5 years old (36-47 lbs) is 10 ml. Everything I'm finding on the internet is saying the dosage for that age & weight is 7.5 ml. 

Why is there a difference between the bottle and kids hospital websites & what dosing should I use? I have always used the 10 ml dosage and just gave my son 10 ml but now am wondering if I'm dosing properly.

Patient information: Age 5
provided_physician_response:
Proper dosage for ibuprofen (Advil) for pediatrics is 10 mg/kg.
So a theoretical 40lb child is 18kg, this 180mg.

Using a concentration of 100mg/5ml, this gives you a dose of 9mL.

Also acetaminophen/Tylenol is 15mg/kg. (Standard concentration is 160mg/5ml)

Also remembered there are max doses and for most pediatrics I still at 400mg max per dose for Ibuprofen.

I just picked up his third prescription for antibiotics in 30 days, and he has had a fever for 6 days now that doesn't completely go away even with multiple fever reducers (it does go down enough that he's comfortable though). Yesterday I noticed he has swollen, bleeding gums and a few ulcer-like sores in the back of his throat which the doctor diagnosed as hand, foot, and mouth disease (no tests were done though). Today I brought him back in due to his fever spiking to 104.6 and him struggling to walk/move last night (also improved - but not completely fixed - with meds) and they did a strep test which came back positive.

The reason I'm really worried though is the weight loss and his medical record in general. I looked up his growth chart when I got home (I can access his records online) and he has grown 1.3 inches in the last 6 months but his weight dropped by 1 pound, causing his BMI to go from the 20th percentile to the 1st. 

I also looked at his blood work. They checked his hemoglobin at his 6-year checkup in July and that was low at 10, but they told me to just make sure he's eating iron (he eats a lot of iron-rich foods but doc said to just increase them). The last time he had a CBC was 5 years ago at his 1 year check-up but I looked at it anyway and his lymphocytes were high and neutrophils were low, but I don't think his doctor ever said anything about abnormal results so maybe that's not a concern? I didn't have online access at the time so I'm sure when they didn't call with results, I assumed they were normal.

Should I have the doctor do a CBC if he keeps getting infections or not gaining weight/losing weight? Or should the doctor tell me if these things are concerning? I feel like a hypochondriac but I really just have a feeling something isn't right. :(

provided_physician_response:
Not likely to be something to stress over.

Though it varies by your community/exposure risks, I have seen multiple cases between the hospital and clinic this last month with multiple viruses, back to back viruses, etc. It is not unreasonable that he was sick multiple times.

The fever is likely from whatever viral processes he had going on.  Outside of strep nothing sounds bacterial from what you've mentioned so I think 3 rounds of antibiotics was more appeasement or risk stratification than "appropriate" treatment.  Without a known or suspected bacterial nidus, no reason for antibiotics.

He could have poorer dental hygiene with being sick, inflammation from infection, or it could be something like a vitamin C deficiency with the bleeding gums and recurrent infections.  Load him up with some emergenC.

Weight loss is normal when being sick and I wouldn't even look at his weight again until he's been healthy for around 4-6 weeks with normal appetite.

HFM is a clinical diagnosis, I wouldn't send you to get the $800+ PCR test to confirm it in just about any case, since the management wouldn't change.

His CBC 5 years ago is has virtually no relevance to his current state unless there was a pathological anomaly like leukemia found on the initial one.  I wouldn't even concern myself with mild anemia in 1-2 year olds at that level due to increased milk consumption and the body still ramping up production while growing rapidly.

At the end of the day nothing here is concerning for him being sick beyond seasonal illness but you should speak to your pediatrician about it in more detail so you feel comfortable that you've covered your bases if you're truly still worried.

My 6-year-old, who I'll call J, is the only kiddo with any issues, and they've generally been mild. She has moderate asthma which is controlled with Flovent, but has otherwise been a healthy and active kid.

But recently, J has been getting sick a LOT. I just picked up her third prescription for antibiotics in 30 days, and she has had a fever for 6 days now that doesn't completely go away even with multiple fever reducers (it does go down enough that she's comfortable though). Yesterday I noticed she has swollen, bleeding gums and a few ulcer-like sores in the back of her throat which the doctor diagnosed as hand, foot, and mouth disease (no tests were done though). Today I brought her back in due to her fever spiking to 104.6 and her struggling to walk/move last night (also improved - but not completely fixed - with meds) and they did a strep test which came back positive.

The reason I'm really worried though is the weight loss and her medical record in general. I looked up her growth chart when I got home (I can access her records online) and she has grown 1.3 inches in the last 6 months but her weight dropped by 1 pound, causing her BMI to go from the 20th percentile to the 1st.

I also looked at her blood work. They checked her hemoglobin at her 6-year checkup in July and that was low at 10, but they told me to just make sure she's eating iron (she eats a lot of iron-rich foods but doc said to just increase them). The last time she had a CBC was 5 years ago at her 1 year check-up but I looked at it anyway and her lymphocytes were high and neutrophils were low, but I don't think her doctor ever said anything about abnormal results so maybe that's not a concern? I didn't have online access at the time so I'm sure when they didn't call with results, I assumed they were normal.

Should I have the doctor do a CBC if she keeps getting infections or not gaining weight/losing weight? Or should the doctor tell me if these things are concerning? I feel like a hypochondriac but I really just have a feeling something isn't right.

Not likely to be something to stress over.

Though it varies by your community/exposure risks, I have seen multiple cases between the hospital and clinic this last month with multiple viruses, back to back viruses, etc. It is not unreasonable that he was sick multiple times.

The fever is likely from whatever viral processes he had going on.  Outside of strep nothing sounds bacterial from what you've mentioned so I think 3 rounds of antibiotics was more appeasement or risk stratification than "appropriate" treatment.  Without a known or suspected bacterial nidus, no reason for antibiotics.

He could have poorer dental hygiene with being sick, inflammation from infection, or it could be something like a vitamin C deficiency with the bleeding gums and recurrent infections.  Load him up with some emergenC.

Weight loss is normal when being sick and I wouldn't even look at his weight again until he's been healthy for around 4-6 weeks with normal appetite.

HFM is a clinical diagnosis, I wouldn't send you to get the $800+ PCR test to confirm it in just about any case, since the management wouldn't change.

His CBC 5 years ago is has virtually no relevance to his current state unless there was a pathological anomaly like leukemia found on the initial one.  I wouldn't even concern myself with mild anemia in 1-2 year olds at that level due to increased milk consumption and the body still ramping up production while growing rapidly.

At the end of the day nothing here is concerning for him being sick beyond seasonal illness but you should speak to your pediatrician about it in more detail so you feel comfortable that you've covered your bases if you're truly still worried.

clinical_context:
45 F. 5'7", 220 lbs, former smoker. Drink occasionally. Nothing recreational. Meds: omeprazole daily, famotidine prn, cetirizine daily. 

I had an abdominal/pelvic CT today for months long issue of epigastric pain radiating to the back. Endoscopy was normal, symptoms not relieved by PPIs or H2 blockers, hence the CT.

My question is regarding an incidental finding on the CT that the GI office did not bring up when they called me to discuss results. I only saw the complete report after getting off the phone.

There was nothing on the CT that could explain my GI symptoms, but under the "Findings" section for lower chest "mild scarring/atelectasis" is listed. No other description is given. However, these findings are left out of the "Impressions" section of the report. As I said, I'm a former smoker. I have also had pneumonia at least 3 times in my life with a bout back in April. I didn't have a chest x-ray until May, a couple of weeks later, and that read "Impression: Peribronchial thickening consistent with bronchiolitis and/or reactive airway disease". No one called me to discuss those particular results and I had mostly recovered from the pneumonia (I thought) so I just shrugged it off. Turns out that since that bout of pneumonia, I have a harder time catching my breath than I used to and it's even a bit painful sometimes depending on the level of strain.

The CT report is verbatim as follows:  "Lower chest: mild scarring/atelectasis"

 Can someone explain to me what this actually might mean for me clinically? Google U just screams "COLLAPSED LUNG" at me and that is not helpful. Is this something I need to be concerned about? What could be the cause? Can it be related to the findings on that x-ray? Should I get a pulmonology consult?

I should add that I am changing insurance plans for the 2nd time in one year and the town I live in has a provider shortage and most of them are only accepting new OB patients. It has been difficult getting care because of this.

Thanks for the input.

Patient information: Age 45, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
Atelectasis isn't an uncommon finding. It just means your lung in that area is not being inflated. It is indeed collapsed. This can be for any number of reason but for most it is due to lack of exercise or activity. It's also common in those with recurrent infections or get bronchitis because gunk builds up and blocks airways from getting proper aeration. Typically when you work your body, you tend to breath in harder which opens up all portions of your lungs. 

Your lungs are made up of tons of tiny little balloons (alveoli). The balloons at the bottom of your lung sometimes need extra force to really open them up. In your case, if you have scarring in that area, it may be even harder to inflate. Atelectasis is when the balloons collapse and haven't been opened up in some time. It looks like your lung tissue has shrunken but typically isn't a problem unless a large portion of your lung is affected. 

If you've never tried one, a spirometer might be beneficial to help open up this portion of your lung. Guaifenesin to clear out mucus may also help. It can also be painful to open that portion of the lung up if atelectasis has been long standing.

{23, Male ; from Belgium}



Hi Everyone !

I hope you are well. As far as I am concerned, I am not fine :/. Indeed, I have had pain in my wrist for almost a year now. The pain appeared after a game of bowling (I don't remember exactly how I got hurt because at the time I didn't feel any pain). At first I thought it was tendonitis, so I rested my wrist, but nothing helped: the pain persisted.

The pain is on the radial side of the wrist. To be precise, I would say that the pain is located in the synovial sheath at the level of the radial extensors. The pain is quite diffuse (from the extensor pollicis longus to the abductor pollicis longus), so it is complicated to determine a precise location of the pain.

The pain is always present to an acceptable degree but it intensifies when I pronate or flex my wrist, for example. Tennis is typically the kind of sport I can't do anymore because the pain is too intense.

A few months ago I had an MRI scan but the radiologists didn't see anything abnormal. I think they must have looked wrong because when I did an ultrasound scan a few weeks later, they told me I had inflammation of the sheath and that an infiltration would solve the problem. The problem is that the cortisone infiltration (done on the radial extensors) that I did, didn't work. So now, I don't know who to believe and I don't know the cause of my pain. I think that maybe the problem is related to the nerves (radial or medial) and not to the tendons  but that's just a guess.

Is there anyone here who could look at my MRI (I'll send you a video) because I'm sure they didn't look properly...



Cheers !

Patient information: Age 23, Gender: M
provided_physician_response:
Sure sounds like tendonitis. Nerve pain in that area would generally not be exacerbated by moving the wrist, though pain with pronation could potentially point to nerve entrapment at the elbow. Any history of elbow injuries?

 The negative MRI is good news that there wasn't anything lurking at the wrist like a missed broken bone. Typically for tendinitis - or pain at the radial wrist for a variety of reasons - a [thumb spica splint](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0B5Q3LBLJ?pd_rd_i=B0B5Q3LBLJ&pf_rd_p=8df9856b-9cff-4e77-9cb1-dc4719b9c19d&pf_rd_r=4MEXZW2FR80E7K1KXMRS&pd_rd_wg=kSfKc&pd_rd_w=WN1Ye&pd_rd_r=0545045d-c9b5-4f0f-bc46-c0ca0633e140) and hand therapy will do the trick, and we only reach for cortisone injections if you've tried those and failed.

Is it possible to lose eyesight and it mean nothing? 22F, 5'6",207lbs, caucausian. One time event. Vape and smoke weed. I work in electrical so considered the possibility of damage from dust. History of bulimia which is currently active (would say 3-4 days are purge days). 

It comes down to last night, on a walk, I got excessively dizzy and weak. I kept on walking with vision in both eyes intermittently disappearing (never both eyes at once) eventually when the weakness peaked (it felt hard to identify words at this point, was on phone call) my left eye lost all vision for about 30 seconds. Afterwards the extreme blur stayed for about two hours. Had a big ol' headache behind the left eye about an hour after vision loss. Still do, pulsing, changing in intensity at random. I'm hoping it's nothing worrisome and really want to know if it is possible that is so. I can't afford a copay til weeks end

Patient information: Age 22, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
Neurosurgeon here.

We use an unnecessarily fancy term for that: amaurosis fugax which means transient vision loss. It results from the retina not getting enough blood flow for a short period of time (the ophthalmic artery is the first to branch from the internal carotid artery and also has collateral flow from the external carotid in some people) and can be considered a stroke symptom, making it a TIA (transient ischemic attack: basically pre-stroke). Though since you're young, I wouldn't put a stenotic ICA or CCA on the top of my list as the "sudden, short and quickly recovered loss of vision" is more commonly a result of your blood pressure being too low for a short period of time. In other words your heart couldn't keep up to your brains oxygen (blood flow) needs for a short while but eventually adjusted, just a little bit late. If the symptom repeats, I would (if I were to see you as a patient in clinic or maybe the ER) refer you to a cardiologist and maybe also consider a brain vessel imaging (a CTA or MRA, whichever is preferred). Considering your history, dehydration may have exacerbated the issue so try to stay hydrated. A syncope event itself is mostly okay as blood flow to the brain is usually immediately recovered but falling down and hitting your head on something like concrete may not.

Overall size measures approximately 8mm. There appears to be incomplete separation of the hemispheres with an apparent cortical defect." Everything else is listed as normal and nasal bone mentioned as identified; but then at the bottom of the report it sums up: "Impression: Single live fetus at 11 weeks 6 days. Abnormal appearance head, cerebrum and cerebellum. Absent nasal bone. Omphalocele." Patient information: Age 34, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
The ultrasound that is performed around 11-13 weeks of pregnancy is very important in order to detect certain abnormalities that can be seen early in pregnancy. The one image you have provided does not help a lot. However, absent nasal septum can be a worrying sign, although not always indicative of an actual problem with the fetus since it can be seen later in pregnancy. I have seen mothers with small noses have fetuses that looked like that on ultrasound but were born completely normal. Regarding the brain abnormalities, some cannot be seen clearly so early in pregnancy and some can be corrected later on. If absence of cerebellum is confirmed however, it can turn out to be a very serious condition for the newborn and can lead to severe developmental delay and neurological problems later in life. 

You should for sure have another ultrasound by a specialist in that field. You might need also further testing, e.g. amniocentesis to confirm. I don't want to sound extremely alarming but you should also think about the possibility of terminating such a pregnancy if severe abnormalities are confirmed. 

Excuse the maybe not so great use of the language but English is not my native language. If you need more clarification feel free to ask. Best of luck to you.

clinical_context: What other kind of testing should I really ask for following my recent admission to the hospital and receiving a negative EEG after multiple fainting episodes?? [23F, Hispanic, 131 lbs, recently diagnosed with vertigo, Vasovagal syncope, and possibly POTS Syndrome, my primary issue has developed quite rapidly over the course of the past week or so] So, I'm feeling very overwhelmed here. I've never been diagnosed with epilepsy, which is a big relief, but I'm still really concerned. I've had doctors toss around the idea of "absence seizures" when I would have spells of zoning out over the past few years, which was pretty unsettling. I also used to faint randomly, but that stopped for a few years. Fast forward to this week, I'm having issues again - and they're much worse. On Monday, I went to the ER because I've been experiencing some really messed up vertigo symptoms. I felt extremely off. They told me the vertigo was related to my blood pressure and heart rate dropping and spiking upon position changes (I think they mentioned POTS?). On Tuesday... I've avoided using excessive capitalization, asterisks, or dramatic prefixes, and preserved the original structure and flow of the post. night: I pass out at home after feeling light headed for a while. This time (unlike times in previous years) I am out, unconscious on the floor. When I wake up I get told my eyes were fluttering and I wasn't responding. I was out maybe 3 minutes. I still had trouble speaking after waking up. Wednesday morning: I got to work, my head was killing me in one specific spot in the back of my head for a few hours. Pain started to get intense, started getting heart palpitations, light headed was returns- BOOM, hit the ground - unconscious yet again. One of my co-workers found me, I wasn't responding and I was randomly twitching. My eyes were open but fluttering again. He called an ambulance and once the medics got there (literally within 2 minutes) they tried to wake me up but I wasn't responding still. I was in and out by this point but I couldn't speak or move. I heard him say my eyes were all over the place, next thing I knew he was digging his knuckles into my sternum and that mostly got me conscious again. When I opened my eyes I was dead confused and felt like I was about to slip out again. They brought me to the hospital and the doctor was ready to chalk it up to a migraine until it happened again while she was right next to me. Then she decided I needed to be seen by neurology and I was admitted. While I waited a few hours for neurology, the nurses noticed my eyes, tried to wake me up but I was again unable to speak or move. More knuckles into my sternum. They got a rush order for an EEG (still took a few hours to get) but they only did it for about 35 mins and that was with breaks because I had to keep using the bathroom. Once the test was done and read- they said it came back normal and that it was not seizures. I was told it was Vasovagal syncope + vertigo and potentially POTS Syndrome. Friday: took day off from work to rest as I felt off still. Today at work: started to get odd sensation in back of my head like a tickle or skin crawling feeling almost that moved into back of my neck. Started to feel a bit of twitchiness. Feeling got more intense in my head and I felt myself checking out again. My co worker made sure I was safe and tried to wake me up. He said my eyes again were all over the place and fluttery, and this time I was super twitchy. He had to give me a few minutes after I was awake again because I still couldn't speak right after. I just got a notification that the EEG report posted to my portal so I looked at it (even though I am aware I was told it was normal). I read it, it says "No epileptiform abnormalities are appreciated"(I.e-normal), but in the beginning of the report it's says "subsequently witnessed to have episode of R head turn and unresponsiveness c/f seizure." I know I'm not a doctor, I have no clue about any of this, but I feel like I need medication. My body feels SO exhausted after every episode and it's draining me.I just need to know what the hell is going on or what I should do. I'm also taking a break from driving for now to be safe. I'm seriously at a loss. It keeps happening and I keep feeling specific things before it happens. Please shed ANY light on this. I have a child to chase around and need to get better. Patient information: Age 23, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
These are atypical symptoms and while I've learned anything can be seizure it can also be other things.

- I'd try my best to keep hydrated, alongside a high salt diet for now to see whether that gets you feeling better. If this helps, would be suggestive of POTS or vasovagal spells (you can youtube "the fainting lark" for examples of passing out that look like seizures).

- agree with not driving for now just in case, as you seem exhausted regardless, even if these aren't seizures

- consider requesting an ambulatory eeg via a neurologist or your doc. You'd essentially just wear an eeg for several days, and since you have these spells frequently, are likely to get an answer 

- empiric seizure med could also be tried. Depends on the doc and their comfort level with trying something but something like topiramate could help both prevent migraines and seizures.

Radom deafness 21F, 120lbs, POTS and FMF taking metoprolol and colchicine 
I'm having my 3rd flare of this issue. In July, I got super bad tinnitus, I couldn't hear anything other than a deep rumbling in my ears. I got a head CT which didn't show anything and it went away after 2 weeks on it's own. In April, it happened again, accompanied with vertigo, and I ended up in the hospital for a week because I also had SVT. Now this week, I'm having it again. It sounds like a motorcycle is idling in my ear. My doctors say it's just probably caused by high blood pressure but I checked and my BP is normal. Is there anything that could better explain why this keeps happening and how to prevent it?

Patient information: Age 21, Gender: F
provided_physician_response:
I'd get a hearing test and consider seeing an ENT. Episodes like this could be related to Meniere's. Classically these are vertigo episodes with hearing loss, ear fullness, and increase in tinnitus that last a few hours, although the dizziness can persist. There are atypical variants though. Other options include migraine. There are some autoimmune causes to fluctuating hearing as well. 

Either way, the starting point is ENT and hearing test.

ECG T-wave inversion? Hello,

I (26M, 179cm, 59kg, no smoking/alcohol/drugs) recently went to a clinic because I tend to black out after mild exertion, (like running to the bus), and had an ECG. The results were apparently a bit unusual with a T-wave inversion in V1-V2. After consulting a cardiologist my Dr. told me this could be a sign of either:

A previous heart attack, or 
A natural phenomenon that can be seen in young, tall, skinny people.

This fascinates me, because those two possibilites feel about as far apart as you could get. While I certainly fit the latter category, severe coronary heart disease runs in the family so I am a bit nervous.

I will be having a bunch of tests done sometime in the near future, but out of curiosity I've been reading about this to try and understand why a result like this could indicate two such different things.

As far as I can gather, the inversion is present after an infarction due to electrically dead scar tissue. But it is also common in children and can sometime remain into early adulthood. I can't find any info on why this happens in kids though, and would be grateful if anyone with some insight could explain.

Thanks!

Patient information: Age 26, Gender: M
provided_physician_response: T-wave inversion in V1 and V2 is completely normal; these leads are supposed to have T-wave inversion.

Dear [Patient's Name],

I understand your concern about hair loss. It is not uncommon for patients undergoing chemotherapy, such as the adjuvant doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide treatment you are currently receiving, to experience hair loss as a side effect. This occurs because chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, which includes both cancer cells and hair follicles.

Here are some recommendations to help minimize hair loss and manage its impact:

1. Be gentle with your hair: Use a soft-bristle brush, avoid tight hairstyles, and minimize the use of heat-styling tools.

2. Consider cutting your hair short: This can make hair loss less noticeable and easier to manage.

3. Use a gentle shampoo and conditioner: Look for products specifically designed for thinning hair or those labeled as "gentle" or "moisturizing."

4. Protect your scalp: Wear a hat or sunscreen when outdoors to protect your scalp from sunburn and other environmental factors.

5. Explore hair coverings: You may want to consider wearing a wig, scarf, or hat to help cope with hair loss. Some insurance plans may cover the cost of a wig, so it's worth checking with your provider.

6. Be patient: Hair loss due to chemotherapy is typically temporary, and your hair should begin to grow back within a few months after completing treatment.

Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have any further questions or concerns. We are here to support you throughout your treatment journey.
